reference.source: Braddom's Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation / pain medicine references
clinicalPearls: Chronic pelvic pain is persistent, non-cyclical pain perceived in the pelvis lasting at least several months and often without a single identifiable structural cause
It frequently reflects overlapping contributions from gynaecological, urological, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, neurological, and psychological systems, so evaluation must be broad
Pelvic floor muscle dysfunction with hypertonicity and myofascial trigger points is a common and treatable contributor that is easily overlooked
Central sensitisation is often present and helps explain pain that is disproportionate to examination findings and associated with other chronic pain conditions
A careful history should screen for endometriosis, interstitial cystitis or bladder pain syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome, pudendal neuralgia, and a history of physical or sexual trauma
Pelvic floor physical therapy is a cornerstone of management, alongside neuropathic pain agents, treatment of identified contributors, and psychological therapies
A multidisciplinary, biopsychosocial approach with realistic functional goals is more effective than repeated searches for a single surgical cause
Trigger-point injection and, in selected cases, nerve blocks such as pudendal blocks may be used within a broader programme
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic pelvic pain typically arises from the interaction of peripheral visceral and somatic nociceptive input with central pain processing changes. Viscero-somatic and viscero-visceral convergence in the spinal cord means input from one pelvic organ can amplify and refer pain to others. Persistent nociception promotes peripheral and central sensitisation, with reduced descending inhibition, so pain becomes self-sustaining and disproportionate to any ongoing tissue damage. Pelvic floor muscle overactivity, myofascial trigger points, and psychological factors including anxiety, depression, and prior trauma further modulate and maintain the pain.
additionalDifferentials: Irritable bowel syndrome or inflammatory bowel disease
Pudendal neuralgia or other nerve entrapment
Chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men
additionalInvestigations: Thorough pelvic and musculoskeletal examination including assessment of pelvic floor tone and trigger points
Urinalysis and targeted urological evaluation for bladder pain syndrome
Pelvic ultrasound and, where indicated, MRI to assess gynaecological and structural causes
Diagnostic laparoscopy in selected cases where endometriosis or adhesions are suspected
Assessment for coexisting mood disorder, sleep disturbance, and central sensitisation
redFlags: Abnormal vaginal or rectal bleeding, postmenopausal bleeding, or a pelvic mass suggesting malignancy
Unexplained weight loss, fever, or night sweats
Acute severe pain with peritonism suggesting a surgical emergency
Haematuria or new bowel symptoms warranting urgent investigation
New neurological deficit in the pelvic or lower limb distribution
reference.prognosis: Chronic pelvic pain often follows a fluctuating long-term course, but many patients achieve meaningful improvement in pain and function with a coordinated multidisciplinary programme that addresses physical, neurological, and psychological contributors. Outcomes are poorer when treatment focuses narrowly on a single organ and ignores central and musculoskeletal factors.
pitfalls: Repeated surgery or invasive procedures in pursuit of a single structural cause when pain is centrally mediated
Overlooking pelvic floor muscle dysfunction as a treatable contributor
Ignoring psychological factors and a history of trauma that maintain the pain
Long-term opioid use, which is generally unhelpful and harmful in this setting
Failing to screen for red-flag features of malignancy or a surgical emergency
management: Pelvic floor physical therapy targeting muscle hypertonicity and myofascial trigger points as a cornerstone of care
Directed treatment of identified contributors such as endometriosis, bladder pain syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome and pudendal neuralgia
Neuropathic pain agents such as antidepressants and anticonvulsants for the centrally sensitised component
Psychological therapies to address central sensitisation, mood and the impact of prior trauma
Interventional measures including pudendal or other nerve blocks and trigger-point injection in selected patients
Diagnostic laparoscopy where endometriosis or adhesions are suspected
Coordinated multidisciplinary management addressing physical, neurological and psychological factors
